titles: South Korea Broke Population Math: 100 Grandparents, Only 4 Great-Grandkids
0.72 Sounds Like Nothing. It Erases 95% of a Nation in 100 Years.
Why Korea's Birth Rate Isn't a Korea Problem: Japan, Italy, China and the US Are 15 Years Behind
primary_title: South Korea Broke Population Math: 100 Grandparents, Only 4 Great-Grandkids
description:
South Korea's fertility rate is 0.72 — a decimal so small it sounds like a rounding error. Run it forward three generations and 100 grandparents leave behind fewer than 5 great-grandchildren, a 95.3% contraction with no war, no famine, and no plague.

This is the arithmetic almost nobody does out loud. Below the 2.1 replacement rate, population math stops behaving like slow decline and starts behaving like reverse compound interest — and Korea just happens to be the first country to reach the part of the curve everyone else is already on.

📊 KEY STATISTICAL TAKEAWAYS
• Korea's total fertility rate fell from 4.53 (1970) to 0.72 (2023), rebounding only slightly to roughly 0.75 in 2024 — with Seoul near 0.55, against a replacement rate of 2.1. In 2018 Korea became the first nation in peacetime history to fall below 1.0 with no war, famine, or plague.
• Statistics Korea's medium projection takes the population from its 51.8M peak down to roughly 36M by 2072, cuts the working-age cohort roughly in half, and pushes the median age from about 45 to the low 60s — collapsing the worker-to-retiree ratio from 5:1 toward 1:1.
• Korea is not an outlier, it's the front of the curve: Japan crossed 1.3 in 2005, Italy hit a record-low ~1.18 in 2024, China fell to roughly 1.0–1.1 as annual births halved from 18.8M (2016) to about 9.5M (2024), and the US recorded a record-low ~1.6. Every one of those lines is already below 2.1.

🔍 SOURCES & METHODOLOGY
• Statistics Korea (KOSTAT) — Birth Statistics and Population Projections for Korea, medium-variant scenario (2072 horizon)
• Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare — Vital Statistics; National Institute of Population and Social Security Research (IPSS)
• ISTAT (Italy) — Natality and fertility indicators, 2024 provisional release
• National Bureau of Statistics of China — annual births and population releases, 2016–2024
• CDC / National Center for Health Statistics — U.S. Births: Provisional Data
• UN World Population Prospects; World Bank Open Data — cross-country fertility comparisons

Methodology note: the generational collapse model is deliberately simplified. Dividing the total fertility rate by 2 yields a per-couple generational multiplier (0.72 ÷ 2 = 0.36 per person, or 0.36 × 2.1 ≈ 0.76 relative to replacement), then compounding it forward across three ~30-year generations. It holds fertility constant and excludes immigration, mortality change, and generational timing shifts — so it is not a forecast of Korea's actual future population. It is a demonstration of what a sub-replacement rate does when compounded, which is exactly the intuition most people lack. Projected figures come from official medium-variant scenarios; all rates are as published at time of production and may be revised.

This video takes no position on causes. The chart doesn't blame housing, working hours, gender politics, or immigration policy — it only shows what the numbers do.
